items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: And I worked with Lucky's band.

ctx.x: So Lucky says, -- Lucky was tight with the union, you know. He's a big man down there. They tell me like during Christmastime, he looked like Santa Claus. He'd go into so many presents, everybody in the union got a big present from him. He didn't care anything about money. I want to tell you some things about Lucky, too, that I think you might like. He was a great man. And he says, "Well, do you want to come to work with me?" He said, "I'm working up to 845," had a hell of a band up there, Joe Wilder and Frank…

played -- had a hell of a brass section, good reed section. I said, "Man, I can't go to work. I'm just putting my transfer in today." I says, "I can't work on a --" He says, "Are you interested?" I says, "Yeah, but you know what happens if they catch me, you know?" They'll tear up your card and maybe won't let you come in the union. He said, "Don't worry about it." Well, I'd heard he was big with the union people. And so I went to work that night, Gary. And I worked six weeks at the 845. Now, I don't have but…

I was getting like two, three record dates a day, three and four record dates, man, because during this time, there were a lot of big bands, you know, like integrated bands, cats was calling me when they knew I was out -- you know, like out in Romeo and those cats in Hymie Schertzef and all them cats, they were giving me rings and all that kind of stuff. So we were doing a lot of things for singers. They still had a lot of singers in those days, big bands and things.

items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: off and on I worked with bands like Lucky Millinder

ctx.x: I’d just like to open with a few questions. I’d like to ask you how did you first get attracted to the field of jazz? And how young were you when you started playing?

Well I must have been about 14, between 14 and 16 years of age. And we had a family band in my home town in Sherman, Texas. And it was a nice little old band, it was a good band, and we would play towns like, well I’d say from Sherman to we’d go to Oklahoma City and Ardmore, Oklahoma, and places like that. And my first professional band that I worked with was with a band called T. Holders Twelve Clouds of Joy, who later became Andy Kirk’s Twelve Clouds of Joy. And I left home with them when I was about, well…
traveling more until I had several health problems, and that cut off the traveling. So that’s where I am today, that’s about it.
